newsitem.title: FINLAND: J & J to market Finnish cholesterol cutting agent.
newsitem.headline: J & J to market Finnish cholesterol cutting agent.

text.p: Johnson & Johnson on Tuesday acquired from a tiny Finnish firm rights to market a dietary ingredient that is patented for use in reducing cholesterol -- and that could eventually find its way into oil-based foods such as salad dressing or even chocolate.
Stanol ester, a plant-derived substance, is currently marketed in Europe in a margarine called Benecol.

Terms of the acquisition of the rights from Finland's Raisio Group were not disclosed. Under the agreement, Johnson & Johnson's McNeil Consumer Products group plans to use stanol ester in a variety of products.
"We are looking at a variety of forms for stanol ester -- food or possibly a drug," said Ron Schmid, a spokesman for McNeil Consumer Products in Fort Washington, Pa.
"There are any number of ways to market this product and once we decide which forms we will go to the proper authorities for approval," he said, including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

Benecol stanol ester, a molecule adapted by Finnish scientists, has been clinically proven to lower blood cholesterol levels. Made mainly from pine trees, it has been on the Finnish market since 1995 in margarine form.

Raisio, whose main Finnish owners are the farmers who provide it with the raw materials for its food business, says Benecol can just as easily be consumed in other fat-containing foods, such as chocolate.
The company, based near the southwestern Finnish town of Turku, said in a statement that McNeil aims to launch the product in spring 1998.
The deal, which also includes Mexico, Canada and Puerto Rico, must be approved by U.S. antitrust authorities.
"Americans have identified cholesterol as one of their leading health concerns," McNeil Consumer Products Chief Executive Brian Perkins said in the Raisio statement.
"We believe that, together with a proper diet and exercise, stanol ester opens up new possibilities for consumers to become more involved in their own health and wellness," Perkins said.
The population of North America is 70 times that of Finland's 5 million, where the annual value of the Benecol market is 90 million markka ($17 million), Raisio said.
Scientists say high blood cholesterol is a key factor in heart disease, the No. 1 world killer accounting for over 6 million deaths worldwide in 1990, according to World Health Organisation figures.
About 950,000 Americans die of heart disease, stroke or hypertensive diseases yearly, according to Centres for Disease Control (CDC) data.

McNeil, which makes Tylenol painkillers, was chosen for its marketing know-how and strong scientific and clinical research, said Raisio. Parent company Johnson & Johnson has annual revenues of over $21.6 billion.
Raisio Vice President Tor Bergman told reporters the company was working on selling Benecol further afield: "Europe and Japan are the next areas, and the work has begun," he said.
Scientists have been looking at plant sterols since the 1950s, knowing they can reduce blood cholesterol levels: Raisio was the first to make them available in fat-soluble form.

A study published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1995 showed an average decline of 10.2 percent in blood cholesterol levels among 153 participants who took Benecol for a year as part of a managed diet.
Johnson & Johnson stock was down $1.1875 at $61.75 in midday trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
